r: This zero-credit course is individual coaching for BFA Music Theatre students: weekly one-and-a-half-hour sessions in which students perform for one another, building toward a live jury performance before faculty. Since the course's pass condition is attendance plus a satisfactory in-person jury, there is no automatable deliverable to intercept. By 2031, AI-generated performance and virtual-production tools will likely be more visible across musical theatre's professional and training contexts, and coaching-adjacent paperwork such as feedback logs could see modest AI assistance. Observed-usage data shows AI adoption concentrated in computer, mathematical, and writing tasks rather than live vocal-physical performance, and diffusion into small-group conservatory-style coaching remains limited given uneven institutional uptake. The jury committee, not a digital artifact, verifies competence, and that verification cannot be delegated to a model. The continuous-enrollment BFA structure is unlikely to loosen within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case for weekly live coaching stays Low across this horizon.

Over a decade, synthetic performance media will grow markedly more convincing and could reshape parts of the musical theatre industry's production economics. That is a labor-market question distinct from whether a BFA candidate still needs coached, embodied rehearsal culminating in a live jury. Capability trend data shows AI task-horizons compounding quickly, yet the central-case trajectory extends AI's reach across digital and analytical tasks well before it displaces the physical, real-time performance instrument this course cultivates, and no plausible path lets a synthetic proxy satisfy an in-person faculty jury. The wide-uncertainty caveat applies most to the surrounding entertainment market, not to the pedagogical requirement itself. Absent an accreditation-level change to BFA jury requirements, which the record gives no indication of, the rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and live human verification.
THE 0010.d: This course is required for all BFA Music Theatre (MT) concentration students until their final Senior Showcase/Jury Performance. This course covers individual instruction in performance studies for Musical Theatre. It requires weekly attendance at a one and one-half hour coaching class in which students perform for one another. At the end of the semester, the student must successfully perform before a faculty jury committee in order to pass the course in addition to required attendance at twelve coaching sessions. Students must enroll during each semester of participation in the BFA (MT) concentration and must receive a "Satisfactory" grade in order to continue in the BFA (MT) concentration.

THE 0011.d: This course is required for all BFA Applied Theatre Technology and Design (ATTD) concentration students until their final Senior Portfolio Showcase. This course covers individual instruction in theatre portfolio development, resume development, and career development. It requires monthly attendance of at least one BFA group meeting and one individual meeting. Students focus on applied musicianship skills including sight-singing, rhythm reading, harmonic recognition, and score analysis. Students will practice learning repertoire efficiently, communicating with music directors, and adapting to a wide range of musical theatre styles. Designed specifically for Musical Theatre majors, this course equips singing actors with the practical tools needed to succeed in both academic and professional rehearsal settings.

THE 1210.d: In this course, students will explore the fascinating world of theatre, gaining a deeper understanding of the live stage, its performers, and the crafts behind each production. Together, we'll journey from ancient performances to today's modern theatre, discovering how theatre has shaped, and been shaped by, cultures around the world. Through discussions, analysis, and hands-on experiences, students will see how theatre brings stories to life, reflects societal values, and sparks powerful conversations across generations.

The rating remains Low at this horizon.

Over a decade, design-planning automation could mature considerably, and diffusion data suggests broader institutional AI adoption by 2036 than today, but stagecraft's instructional core is the physical skill of building, rigging, and running technical elements safely — tasks that remain embodied and site-specific regardless of how capable planning software becomes. THE 1240.d: Students are introduced to the principles, methods, and materials of technical production, including scenic design and construction, lighting design and practices, and costuming and sound practices.

At 24 months the instrumental need to develop one's vocal instrument through live coaching is unaffected by AI capability.

The embodied, real-time nature of vocal training and its role as a prerequisite foundation for subsequent theatre voice and performance work keep the requirement in place. Diffusion of capable AI vocal coaching into small in-person conservatory-style classes is likely to remain limited within a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low across this horizon.

The course's foundational role feeding into further voice and performance coursework also continues to anchor it in the required sequence. The wide-uncertainty caveat here concerns how much of solo practice time is AI-mediated, not whether the embodied, coached core of vocal training is still instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, grounded in embodiment, verification burden, and foundational sequencing.
THE 2201.d: This course teaches voice users how to develop and use their vocal instruments in public performance environments. This course emphasizes that voice work is for everybody.

THE 2215.d: This course introduces the principles and strategies at one's disposal to live a fulfilling life in the arts. Students learn health and wellness techniques in physical fitness, intimacy, EDI sensitivity, and the collaborative skills of working with various people and personalities.

r: Prison Arts examines the U.S. prison system as a set of social relations and investigates the role of performing arts within retributive, restorative, and transformative justice, asking students to critically reflect on their own intentions in socially-based arts practice. That high-stakes, ethically fraught character keeps a human instructor's judgment necessary regardless of how well AI drafts related text. THE 2218.d: The course provides a background into the culture and logic of the United States prison system, analyzing the prison as a complex set of social relations that both "reform" and "perform." Students investigate the compositional, ideological, and aesthetic dimensions of retributive, restorative, and transformative justice as manifest in the U.S. prison system. This examination has a particular focus on the role of the performing arts in each of these approaches to justice. Students reflect critically on their own intentions and interest in socially-based arts practice, with particular focus on "mutuality." We continue to interrogate the questions: What happens when the prison encounters the artist? What happens when the artist encounters the prison?

THE 2220.d: This course provides an introduction to the basic principles of acting, including improvement of voice, body, and mind in the discipline of the theatre. Particular emphasis is placed on the principles of stage movement, improvisation, and beginning scene work.

THE 2230.d: This course builds upon basic principles of acting, including improvisation, character development, stage movement, voice, and scene work. Study topics include development of audition techniques, basic acting, television acting techniques, and advanced scene work.

But the psychomotor task at this course's core, precise, real-time manual application to a live performer's face, adjusted for lighting, proximity, and movement, is not one AI executes on the student's behalf, and no plausible capability trajectory changes that a person must still physically apply the makeup. The wider uncertainty is about how digital tools reshape the surrounding design and product-selection workflow in the industry, not whether the hands-on application skill this course builds remains necessary. The rating holds Low across the horizon; embodiment is the durable protective factor even as adjacent creative-planning tasks become more AI-assisted, and even as capability elsewhere in visual and generative media continues to advance quickly.
THE 2242.d: This course provides an introduction to the principles, methods, and materials of stage makeup. Students learn to execute a variety of makeup techniques, including base makeup, aging, and special effects to create makeup designs for both realistic and stylized characters.

r: Graphics for Theatre builds hand drafting, perspective, freehand sketching, and rendering technique, preparing students to produce visual design documentation for professional theatre and entertainment work. The applied task blends manual drawing skill with visual communication of technical design intent, a hybrid of psychomotor craft and representational output. Rendering and drafting sit closer to the visual-production tasks that generative image and CAD-assisted tools are increasingly competent at, but the course's foundation is hand-executed technique feeding a design sequence that begins with THE 1240. Task-exposure research finds programming and content-generation tasks most positively exposed, while hands-on execution remains comparatively protected; this course sits between those poles. At 24 months, AI rendering tools exist but are not displacing the foundational hand-drafting instruction a design student needs; the instrumental need for the course is intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted rendering and generative visualization tools will likely be commonplace in entertainment design pipelines, letting designers produce polished visual concepts faster. This raises real exposure for the rendering-output portion of the course's content, since generating a finished rendering is closer to the kind of visual-generation task AI increasingly handles well. However, the course's foundational purpose, teaching a student to draft, understand perspective, and communicate design intent by hand, still requires the human doing the learning, and it remains prerequisite scaffolding for the technical-design sequence. Verification of technical accuracy in a working drawing still benefits from a designer who understands the underlying drafting logic, not just a generated image. On balance the instrumental need softens but does not disappear; the rating reflects meaningfully increased but not dominant exposure at this horizon.

Over a decade, generative rendering and AI-assisted CAD tools are plausible to become standard in entertainment design workflows, consistent with the fast capability-doubling trend observed in current research, potentially absorbing a large share of the finished-rendering task this course partially trains toward. The countervailing factor is that Graphics for Theatre also teaches foundational drafting literacy, perspective, scale, technical communication, that underlies a student's ability to direct, evaluate, and correct AI-generated design output, keeping some instrumental value even as automation rises. This is the most exposed of the production-craft courses in this batch precisely because its output, visual renderings, is digital and representational rather than purely embodied. The rating moves to Medium at this horizon with real uncertainty about how much hand-drafting instruction survives as a distinct requirement.
THE 2243.d: This is an introductory course in graphics for theatre. The student will become familiar with hand drafting, perspective, freehand sketching and rendering techniques through theoretical and practical projects. These skills will prepare the student to incorporate the techniques into professional design and technology work within the theatre and entertainment industry.

r: Wardrobe Technology for Everyone introduces costume design, costume technology, hair and makeup application, and wardrobe management to majors and non-majors alike, emphasizing practical, hands-on application over theory. The applied tasks, fitting a costume, applying makeup, managing a wardrobe track backstage during a run, are manual, in-person, and performed on or with a live human body under production time pressure. Task-exposure research places this kind of physical, tactile execution among the least automatable categories, distinct from the writing and coding tasks research finds most exposed. AI styling-suggestion tools exist, but they do not perform wardrobe changes, apply makeup, or manage a costume plot backstage. Because the course is designed for broad accessibility rather than as a majors-only gateway, it carries no strong scaffolding claim, but embodiment alone keeps the 24-month instrumental need fully intact.

By 2031, some planning-stage tasks, inventory tracking, styling mood boards, scheduling fittings, may be lightly assisted by AI tools embedded in production-management software, offering modest augmentation. That does not reach the applied core this course teaches: hands-on costume fitting, makeup application, and live wardrobe management during a production run, all of which require physical presence and human judgment under real-time conditions. Verification of whether a quick-change worked, or a fit is stage-ready, depends on a person doing the work, not an automated check. Broader survey evidence indicates AI adoption within small production-craft workflows remains uneven and slower than headline capability suggests. The instrumental case for hands-on wardrobe competence remains Low across a catalog cycle; digital tools may streamline planning without touching the physical task.

A decade out, production-management software will likely be more AI-integrated for inventory, scheduling, and design reference generation, but the physically embodied tasks at this course's center, dressing, fitting, and managing wardrobe on live performers in real time, are not the kind of task a language or generative-image model performs. Because the course was not built as prerequisite scaffolding for a specific major sequence, no institutional lock reinforces the rating, but embodiment alone is sufficient protection under the central capability case. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much administrative and planning work around wardrobe management becomes AI-assisted, not whether the hands-on skill remains necessary. The rating holds Low at this horizon, consistent with other embodied production-craft courses in the department and unaffected by the broader pace of capability growth elsewhere.
THE 2248.d: This course provides students with an introduction to the principles, methods, and materials of costume design, costume technology, hair and makeup application, and wardrobe management as it applies to both costume and non-costume focused majors. Emphasis is placed on practical knowledge and application.

r: Dramaturgy trains students to research and provide a production team with historical context, textual analysis, and background knowledge on classic, contemporary, musical, and new plays, then communicate that research to designers, directors, actors, and technicians. This is desk-based research and writing work, gathering information, synthesizing it, and documenting findings for others, performed at a keyboard rather than in embodied rehearsal space. Task-exposure research finds writing and research-synthesis tasks among the most positively exposed categories, and observed usage data shows writing and office-style tasks prominent in current AI use. Current tools can already draft historical background or summarize a play's production history competently. At 24 months, though, dramaturgical judgment about what context a specific production needs is still developing in students, and full deployment of AI research assistants in production dramaturgy is not yet standard practice, keeping the rating Low for now.

By 2031, AI research and synthesis tools will plausibly be routine aids for dramaturgical background work, compiling historical context, cross-referencing textual variants, drafting program notes, meaningfully reducing the labor-intensive research portion of the role. Verification burden here is moderate rather than severe: a dramaturg can generally check a summary against primary sources without the adversarial, high-error-cost conditions seen in clinical or safety fields, so expert oversight is less protective than in embodied disciplines. No licensure or general-studies designation locks this course in place. The collaborative-facilitation piece of dramaturgy, synthesizing perspectives across a production team in person, remains harder to automate than the research itself. On balance, the instrumental case shifts to Medium: AI plausibly handles a substantial share of the research tasks even as the interpretive and facilitation work persists.

Over a decade, given the pace of capability growth in research synthesis and long-context document analysis, AI tools are plausible to competently perform most of the literature review, historical contextualization, and background-compilation work that has traditionally defined entry-level dramaturgy, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing- and research-heavy work is strongly positively exposed. The interpretive judgment about what a specific production needs and the in-person facilitation of a creative team likely persist longer, but they represent a shrinking share of the course's traditionally taught content. With no institutional lock protecting the course and embodiment largely absent from its tasks, the central case points to High exposure by 2036, tempered by real uncertainty about whether production teams keep valuing a human synthesizer of context over a direct AI query.
THE 2255.d: In this course, students learn the skills of dramaturgy in several distinct functions, including how to provide the cast and crew with vital knowledge, research, and historical context about the theatrical work. Students work with classic, contemporary, musical, and new plays, facilitating collaboration between theatre artists (i.e. designers, directors, actors, technicians, and audience). Students practice skills transferable to other theatre disciplines.

r: Production Analysis introduces season selection, production roles, design processes, and the communication dynamics that coordinate a production team across design, direction, and technical departments. Part of the task is analytical and documentary, comparing scripts for season fit, mapping production roles and processes, while another part is coordinating people in real time across departments, a task that requires reading a room and managing collaborative dynamics in person. Task-exposure research finds coordination and interpersonal-management tasks less exposed than pure writing or analysis work, though planning documentation itself is more exposed. AI tools can already help compare scripts or draft process documentation, but the course's synthesis of analytical and interpersonal-coordination skill is still primarily learned through in-person practice. At 24 months the instrumental need remains largely intact, with only the documentary sub-tasks showing early exposure.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly assist more of the analytical and documentation side of production planning, comparing season options, drafting process outlines, tracking design-team communication logs, meaningfully augmenting the planning workflow. The interpersonal coordination piece, managing the communication dynamics between designers, directors, and technicians on an actual production, is harder to substitute and keeps a verification burden tied to real relationships and real deadlines. No institutional mandate locks this course, so the analytical portion's exposure is not offset by a hard external floor. On balance the rating shifts to Medium: a meaningful share of the course's analytical content is plausibly AI-assisted by this horizon, even as the coordination-and-communication skill the course also builds remains comparatively protected and still needs direct practice.

Over a decade, AI-assisted planning and documentation tools could plausibly handle much of the comparative and process-mapping analysis this course teaches, consistent with the general trend of increasing capability in structured analytical tasks. What likely persists is the interpersonal coordination competence, reading and managing the communication dynamics of a live production team, since that remains an in-person, relationship-dependent skill outside AI's current or plausible near-term reach. The course sits in a genuinely mixed position: partially exposed analytical content, partially protected coordination content, with no accreditation or general-studies lock to anchor it. The central-case rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High, reflecting real uncertainty about how much of production planning shifts to AI-assisted tools versus how much remains people-management practice.
THE 2270.d: This course provides an introduction to the principles, methods, and materials of theatre production, including season selection, production roles, design processes, and the communication dynamics within the production team.

r: Theatre Career Development teaches resume and cover-letter writing, interview preparation, website and social-media branding, personal finance management, union membership, and contract negotiation for entering the professional arts field. Much of this content, drafting a resume, writing a cover letter, building website copy, planning a social-media brand, is exactly the kind of writing and self-presentation task that current AI tools already perform competently and that observed-usage data shows is heavily represented in real-world AI use. Productivity research on professional writing tasks shows substantial time savings with quality gains when AI assists drafting, and verification burden for this content is low: a student or advisor can check a generated resume with minimal expertise. The interviewing and negotiation components retain a real-time, human element, but the course's dominant content is already meaningfully automatable, yielding a Medium rating even at 24 months.

By 2031, AI writing assistants will plausibly be the default way students draft resumes, cover letters, and personal branding content, and career-services offices are likely to have normalized AI-assisted application materials, consistent with observed productivity gains in professional writing tasks and low verification burden for this kind of output. Interview practice and negotiation simulation may also become AI-assisted through conversational tools, further compressing the instructional need for structured classroom coverage of these skills. No institutional lock, licensure requirement, or foundational role in a required sequence protects this course from that shift. The interpersonal, real-time components of interviewing and networking remain somewhat more durable, but they represent a shrinking share of the course's content. The rating moves to High, reflecting that most of what the course teaches is now well within AI's competent and adopted range.

Over a decade, the specific administrative and writing tasks this course centers on, application materials, branding content, contract literacy, are plausible candidates for near-complete AI assistance given the capability trend in language tasks and the low verification burden involved in checking such output, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing tasks are among the most positively exposed to AI. What likely remains valuable is judgment about career strategy and live interpersonal negotiation, but the course as currently structured teaches primarily the writing and self-presentation tasks that automate most readily. The central-case rating stays High at this horizon, with the standard hedge that if career-services norms shift toward requiring demonstrated human-only competencies, the course's content could be reoriented rather than eliminated, a possibility this instrumental rating does not fully capture.
THE 2280.d: This course provides an introduction to the principles and practice of entering into the professional field in the arts, including resume and cover letter writing, interviewing, websites, social media branding, personal finance management, becoming a member of a union, negotiating contracts, establishing a strong work ethic, and living a sustainable life in the arts field. Students practice and apply skills through course activities that provide a bridge to their professional career.

r: Stage Combat trains basic techniques in unarmed, broadsword, and rapier-and-dagger stage fighting, with safety as the organizing principle and the goal of making violence look real while keeping actor-combatants physically safe. This is an intensely embodied, real-time psychomotor skill requiring a trained instructor to supervise choreography, timing, and safety protocol on a partner's body, precisely the category of physical, high-stakes, in-person task that task-exposure research places furthest from AI's reach. Verification burden is severe: an error in weapon handling or timing can injure a performer, so oversight strictly requires an instructor who holds this embodied knowledge, not an automated check. No AI system can supervise live weapon choreography or catch an unsafe distance between combatants in real time. At 24 months the instrumental need for hands-on, supervised training is completely intact.

By 2031, AI tools might assist with choreography planning, notation, or reference footage for stage combat sequences, offering marginal support to the design phase. That does not touch the applied core this course teaches: live, supervised physical training in safe weapon handling and unarmed technique, where an instructor's real-time correction prevents injury. The severe verification burden here, a missed correction has physical consequences, keeps a trained human supervisor structurally necessary, and no plausible AI deployment substitutes for in-person safety oversight during weapons choreography. Diffusion of AI into physically supervised performance training is essentially nonexistent given current adoption patterns in even administratively simpler domains. Across a catalog cycle the supervised hands-on training model is unlikely to change. The instrumental case remains Low; the safety-critical embodiment of the task is the durable protective factor.

Even under an aggressive capability scenario for 2036, the core task of Stage Combat, a human instructor supervising live, safety-critical weapon and unarmed combat choreography on another human body in real time, is not one a generative or reasoning AI model performs, regardless of how sophisticated its planning or notation assistance becomes. The severe verification burden intrinsic to physical safety training means expert human oversight is structurally required, not merely currently preferred, which is a stronger protection than convenience-based verification in desk-based fields. The plausible decade-scale change is better AI-assisted choreography planning or virtual previsualization tools, not substitution of the supervised physical training itself. The rating holds Low with high confidence, among the most durably protected courses in the department given the combination of embodiment and injury-risk verification burden.
THE 2290.d: This is an introductory class that addresses basic stage combat techniques and early historical weapons: unarmed, broadsword, and rapier and dagger. The class emphasizes safety first. It also address the challenges of making a fight believable and effective. The actor-combatant must not only act the scene but must also master the various techniques to create the illusion of real violence for the audience.

r: Comedy: In-Print and On-Stage examines the cultural, historical, and literary development of comedy across stand-up, sketch, and staged theatrical forms, asking students to analyze societal and cultural influences on the genre. This is desk-based humanities work, reading, historical research, and interpretive writing about texts and performance traditions, the kind of content-analysis task that task-exposure research associates with meaningfully higher exposure than embodied studio courses, since it involves neither physical craft nor real-time interpersonal performance. The course carries a GT-AH1 general-studies designation, meaning it fulfills Colorado's statutory gtPathways transfer core, a genuine institutional mandate that anchors enrollment regardless of AI capability. AI tools can already draft competent literary-historical analysis of comedic texts. At 24 months the GT transfer requirement is the operative constraint, keeping demand for the course intact even as its analytical content shows early exposure.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly produce competent literary-historical analysis of comedic texts and traditions, meaningfully increasing exposure of the course's core intellectual content relative to embodied studio courses. Verification burden for humanities interpretation is moderate, a student's or instructor's own judgment can generally assess whether an argument is well-supported without high-stakes expert gatekeeping, so the dampening effect of verification is limited here. What holds the rating down is institutional: the GT-AH1 designation ties this course into the statutory gtPathways general-education transfer core, a structural requirement that does not turn on AI capability and does not relax within a catalog cycle. The rating is capped at Medium by that transfer mandate even though the underlying task exposure trend, absent the designation, would point higher.

Over a decade, given the strong association between writing- and analysis-heavy coursework and AI exposure, the underlying content of this course, literary and cultural interpretation of comedic texts, is a plausible candidate for substantial AI competence, and absent any lock the base trajectory would point toward High. But the GT-AH1 general-studies designation is a genuine structural floor: gtPathways is a statutory transfer requirement that changes on legislative rather than technological timescales, and it caps the course's rating at Medium even under an aggressive capability scenario. The real uncertainty is whether gen-ed transfer frameworks themselves get restructured over a decade-plus horizon, which is a policy question outside this rating's scope. The rating holds Medium, driven by institutional lock rather than task protection.
THE 2295.d: This course explores the cultural, historical, and literary aspects of comedy through the lens of the art of theatre. Students learn about societal inspirations for comedy, cultural factors that influence the development of comedy, and how comedy as an art form has developed into modern-day theatrical settings, including stage performance, stand-up comedy, sketch comedy, and others.

r: This survey course asks students to trace musical theatre's evolution from 1888 to the present, analyzing how commercial hits reshaped audience expectations and how the form absorbed vaudeville, jazz, and pop influences over a century. Students are explicitly not required to perform; the applied work is research, historical synthesis, and written argument about well-documented, heavily archived material, tasks mapped to O*NET's information-interpreting and documenting activities. Task-exposure research classifies writing and information-synthesis work as strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and general-purpose models already draft competent narrative histories of popular culture given how thoroughly this subject is digitized and discussed online. Verification stakes are modest: a factual slip in a survey essay is low-cost and easily caught. With no clinical or licensure requirement gating the course and no live-performance component providing embodied protection, the instrumental case for a strictly human-taught route through this material is already measurably eroding at 24 months.

By 2031, AI systems will more fluidly generate and update comprehensive narratives of musical theatre history, potentially incorporating newly digitized archives and pulling together secondary scholarship faster than a student working alone. Observed-usage patterns already show writing and research-adjacent tasks concentrated among the most-used AI applications, and models' growing reasoning depth should make synthesizing a century-plus of theatrical development a still more tractable output. The course's binding constraint remains weak: there is no accreditation floor, licensure requirement, or performance component forcing embodied practice, and the general studies field is empty, so no gen-ed transfer mandate holds it in place. Verification burden stays low because errors in a popular-history survey rarely carry real consequence. The main hedge is that instructors may still value close reading and original argumentation over AI-assisted synthesis, but the instrumental need for the course to convey this factual and interpretive content is meaningfully diminished by this horizon.

Extrapolating a decade out is necessarily uncertain, but the central-case trajectory of capability growth, with task-time horizons compounding every few months per METR/Epoch tracking, points toward AI systems that can produce polished, well-sourced historical and critical narratives about musical theatre with little friction. Nothing about this course's content resists that: it is textual, extensively documented, and not gated by licensure, clinical hours, or embodied performance requirements. If diffusion of these tools into humanities instruction and independent learning continues even at the currently slow, uneven pace documented in adoption surveys, the case for requiring a dedicated course to transmit this material weakens further. The genuine uncertainty concerns institutional pedagogy and enrollment choices rather than raw capability; programs may keep the course for disciplinary reasons even as the instrumental automation case strengthens. The rating reflects task exposure only, not a claim about the course's educational or disciplinary value.
THE 2299.d: Students will be exposed to the most popular theatrical form: Musical Theatre. This exciting American theatrical revolution has transformed how the world views theatre, and how audiences have influenced and been influenced by this creation. Students study the history of this art form from 1888 to the present day. Students are not required to perform.

r: This course trains actors to produce accurate, performance-ready accents and dialects through embodied vocal work, building on IPA mastery from prerequisite phonetics coursework. The applied task is live, real-time vocal production and coached refinement, an instructor listening to a student's articulation and correcting placement, breath support, and prosody in the room. That work maps to O*NET's performing-for-the-public and interpersonal-communication activities, categories task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable because they require psychomotor execution and live human judgment. Speech-recognition and pronunciation apps exist, but they evaluate acoustic accuracy, not the embodied craft of sustaining a believable accent through a scene under performance pressure. Verification burden is real: only a trained ear can judge whether a dialect reads as authentic rather than caricature. At 24 months, nothing in current AI deployment substitutes for the coached, in-person vocal training this course delivers.

By 2031, AI dialect-coaching apps and acoustic feedback tools will likely be more refined, and some rehearsal-adjacent prep work may shift toward AI-assisted drilling. But the instrumental purpose of this course, developing a performer's live, embodied control over voice and speech under real audience or camera conditions, is not something a model performs on the student's behalf. Verification remains human: judging whether an accent reads as authentic, sustains under improvisation, and serves character requires a trained ear making real-time qualitative calls, the kind of non-obvious-failure judgment that keeps expert oversight necessary. No accreditation or gen-ed mandate protects the course, but embodiment alone does the protective work here. Diffusion of capable AI voice tools into everyday production will not have restructured how actors are trained to embody accents by this horizon; the course's instrumental necessity is essentially undiminished.

A decade out, synthetic voice and real-time dialect-modification tools could plausibly be sophisticated enough to alter a recorded performance's accent in post-production, a genuine wide-uncertainty consideration for the voice-over and screen-acting labor market. But that capability changes what happens to a recording after a performance, not whether a live theatre performer needs to embody a convincing accent while acting, breathing, and reacting in real time on stage. The applied skill this course builds, coached, in-person vocal craft, remains outside what generative systems execute for the student. The honest hedge concerns adjacent markets, not this specific instrumental question: even under an aggressive capability scenario, live embodied performance training keeps its function. The rating holds Low across the decade, anchored by embodiment and the irreducibly human verification of live vocal performance quality.
THE 3201.d: This course continues the process of teaching speakers how to use the voice more effectively by beginning dialect exploration through learning and mastering the International Phonetic Alphabet (I.P.A.).

r: This course teaches commercial, narration, and character voice-over technique together with microphone placement and recording-software operation, a hybrid of embodied vocal performance and studio technology. Unlike stage acting, the deliverable is a recorded digital audio file produced solo in a booth rather than live presence before an audience, which weakens the embodiment protection that shields other performance courses. Text-to-speech and voice-cloning tools are already commercially deployed for some narration, IVR, and lower-tier commercial reads, an observed instance of the automation trend the Anthropic Economic Index documents across office and creative tasks. Verification burden is moderate: clients judge tone, brand fit, and character nuance, which still rewards trained human interpretation, especially for higher-end character and dramatic reads. At 24 months, the instrumental need to learn traditional voice-over technique is real but already partially contested by synthetic-voice adoption at the commercial-read tier.

By 2031, synthetic voice generation should be markedly more capable and more broadly adopted for narration, commercial reads, and lower-stakes character work, consistent with the trajectory implied by rapid capability growth documented in task-time-horizon research. The parts of this course centered on microphone technique and recording-technology operation are themselves increasingly mediated by AI-assisted production tools. What likely persists longer is nuanced character interpretation and brand-specific creative judgment, where verification burden is higher because a poor read has real commercial cost, keeping a trained human voice valuable at the premium tier. No accreditation or gen-ed designation protects this course, and its embodiment is only partial since the product is a digital recording, not live presence. The instrumental case shifts from foundational toward specialized: students likely still need this training, but for a narrower, higher-skill segment of the voice-over market.

Over a decade, voice-cloning and generative audio are plausible candidates for handling a large share of routine commercial and narration work, given how much of the underlying task, producing a polished digital audio deliverable from a script, sits inside AI's expanding frontier. The genuine uncertainty is where the line settles: character voice work, branded creative direction, and highly interpretive performance may retain a human-verification premium even as routine reads are commoditized. This course's content, micing, recording technique, and delivery, sits closer to the exposed end of the theatre curriculum precisely because its output is fully digital and remotely producible, unlike live stage work. The rating holds High with real hedging: the central case points toward substantial displacement of entry-level voice-over work, though the ceiling on top-tier creative voice performance remains genuinely unresolved.
THE 3202.d: This course teaches techniques used in the voice-over industry, including commercial, narration, and character recording. Students expand their vocal skill, explore further use of vocal variety and interpretation, in addition to learning microphone technique and recording technology.

r: Scene painting is bench-craft: mixing color, executing faux finishes and trompe l'oeil illusion, and applying texture across large physical scenic units built for a specific production. The applied work is manual and material, brush handling, surface preparation, and iterative visual judgment made standing at the paint frame, mapping to O*NET's handling-objects and physical-activity categories that task-exposure research consistently places at the low-exposure end, far from the programming and writing tasks most associated with AI use. Image-generation tools can produce a rendering of a painted flat, but they cannot execute the physical technique of laying faux-finish glazes on an actual scenic surface for an actual show. Verification is inherently hands-on: an instructor evaluates finish quality by looking at and touching the physical result. With no gen-ed designation and a fully embodied applied task, the instrumental need to learn this physical craft is unaffected at 24 months.

By 2031, digital previsualization and AI-assisted color and rendering tools will likely be more integrated into scenic design workflows, helping designers plan a paint treatment before it is executed. That augments planning, not execution; someone still has to physically mix, layer, and apply paint to a three-dimensional set piece under production deadlines, and that remains outside what a generative model performs. The verification burden stays protective: judging whether a faux marble or trompe l'oeil illusion reads correctly from house seats requires an embodied, spatial assessment no digital tool substitutes for the trained eye and hand together. No accreditation or transfer mandate anchors the course, so embodiment alone carries the weight, but it does so reliably here. The instrumental case for learning physical scene-painting technique remains essentially intact across this horizon; the surrounding design process, not the execution task, is what changes.

A decade out, more of the design and planning side of scenic art, color studies, texture mockups, client presentations, will plausibly be AI-assisted, and the wide-uncertainty caveat about production-pipeline change in professional scenic studios is real. But the specific instrumental task this course teaches, physically executing paint technique on a real scenic surface for a live production, remains a psychomotor, materials-handling activity outside AI's substitutive reach even under an aggressive capability scenario; robots capable of nuanced faux-finish painting on theatrical scenery are not a credible near-term production reality. The rating holds Low through 2036 because the binding constraint is embodiment itself, not an institutional or verification factor that could erode. If anything, as digital pre-visualization absorbs more planning work, the physical execution skill this course builds becomes a comparatively larger share of what a working scenic artist contributes by hand.
THE 3210.d: The student will learn and develop basic and advanced theatrical scene painting skills. This course will focus on techniques of texture, color mixing, faux finishes and trompe l'oeil painting, and the painting of a variety of scenic pieces.

The rating reflects task-level exposure, not a claim that theatre history stops mattering; it holds at the upper band with the calibrated hedge appropriate to a ten-year horizon.
THE 3211.d: As a part of a two semester sequence, this course provides detailed and intensive study of specific theatre contexts, practices, genres, and theories from its "origins" of theatre through 1636.

The genuine hedge concerns interpretive depth: contemporary performance theory and cultural criticism include contested, evolving debates where a single AI-generated synthesis may flatten disagreement that trained instruction surfaces deliberately. That caveat tempers but does not reverse the direction of the estimate. The rating holds at the upper band across the decade, reflecting sustained, text-based task exposure with no institutional brake to hold it down.
THE 3212.d: As a part of a two semester sequence, this course provides detailed and intensive study of specific theatre contexts, practices, genres, and theories from the Neoclassicists to the present.

THE 3213.d: Students use theatre history, dramatic texts, and live performance to explore cultures of previously and/or presently marginalized peoples in order to promote greater understanding of their struggles. The rating holds Low through 2036, anchored by embodiment; the labor-market exposure of movement-based performance work is a separate question from whether a student still needs this course to acquire the underlying physical competence.
THE 3220.d: This course instructs students in the use and training of the human body for communication of artistic expression.

Verification burden stays protective: the ensemble discovers what works only through live rehearsal in the room, an iterative human process. No accreditation or gen-ed mandate applies, so the Low rating continues to rest entirely on embodiment and interpersonal collaboration holding across this horizon. Nothing in the diffusion of AI tools into theatre-adjacent creative work by 2031 plausibly substitutes for the lived, ensemble-based devising experience this course is built to teach.

The instrumental heart of the course, collaborative, embodied ensemble creation culminating in a live original performance, remains outside what AI executes for students even under an aggressive capability scenario, because devising is defined by synchronous human negotiation and live presence, not by the production of source text alone. THE 3222.d: In this course students learn about the history, process, and production involved with devising a theatrical performance. They learn valuable skills in collaboration, activism, and ensemble performance. This class culminates in a final presentation comprised of entirely original work.

The wide-uncertainty caveat concerns how choreography is taught and preserved, not whether a performer still needs to physically learn and execute it. The rating holds Low through 2036; embodiment is a durable protective factor here regardless of capability growth in adjacent generative-media domains.
THE 3224.d: This course is designed to give the aspiring musical theatre performer a basic understanding of the different styles of dance used throughout the canon of Musical Theatre. Students will learn and perform choreography from musicals such as Oklahoma, Anything Goes, West Side Story, A Chorus Line, 42nd Street, etc. Throughout the course, we will learn the original choreography of seminal Broadway choreographers, such as Jerome Robbins and Bob Fosse. We will also practice audition techniques, and how to conduct oneself in rehearsal. In order to execute the choreography of these incredible artists, students will be learning several forms of dance including: ballet, jazz, and ballroom. We will also explore audition techniques as well as how to conduct oneself in rehearsal. Along with learning and executing choreography from various musicals, the students will also study and analyze these musicals in regards to their historical context; the artists involved in making the show; and its impact on the evolution of the American Musical Theatre. This course is designed to create a thinking dancer, who is knowledgeable about the performative aspects of dance in musical theatre, as well as the history of the art form and the artist who have made it.

r: This advanced course builds embodied period-style technique -- basic mask work plus performance conventions particular to Greek theatre, Comedy of Manners, and Shakespeare -- extending the vocal, physical, and interpretive skills students carry from the prerequisite acting sequence. Verification of stylized performance quality is inherently a human, in-person judgment -- an audience's or coach's read of embodied specificity -- keeping oversight tied to expert presence rather than automatable review. Diffusion data shows AI adoption concentrated in knowledge-work firms, not studio arts instruction, and nothing in the capability trajectory changes what a mask or Shakespeare scene requires physically. The instrumental case for enrolling in this course to acquire the technique stays Low, with the caveat that adjacent screen and streaming performance markets are shifting faster than the pedagogy itself.

Over a decade, generative video and synthetic performance will likely be routine in film and some stage-adjacent media, and the capability trend documented by METR/Epoch implies substantially longer-horizon AI competence by 2036 than exists today. Even granting that wide uncertainty, the specific task this course teaches -- a human performer's live, embodied command of period style in front of scene partners -- is not the kind of task those systems perform on the student's behalf; they change the entertainment economy surrounding acting, not the pedagogical necessity of physically learning it. No licensure or accreditation lock is doing the protective work here, embodiment is. The rating holds Low with real hedging about how much the broader performance labor market looks like by 2036, but not about whether the applied classroom task remains something only rehearsed bodies can accomplish.
THE 3230.d: This course is for advanced performers exploring basic "mask" acting techniques, as well as acting styles particular to Greek, Comedy of Manners, and Shakespeare.

r: This course teaches character mask, neutral mask, half-mask, and clowning, explicitly framed as storytelling through the body alone -- communicating objective, circumstance, and reaction without reliance on spoken language. That description makes the applied task unusually pure psychomotor performance: physical listening, spatial awareness, and non-verbal expressive precision developed through repeated in-person exercise and instructor correction. The instrumental case for this course stays Low across the horizon; the hedge is about how mask and physical-theatre technique gets applied professionally, not about whether the embodied skill itself is still worth acquiring in person.

That shift does not touch the instrumental logic of this specific course: teaching a human to generate wordless physical storytelling through their own body is categorically different from an animation pipeline generating a character's movement. The uncertainty genuinely widens over ten years about how physical-theatre graduates are employed and where mask technique gets applied professionally, and that uncertainty should be held honestly rather than resolved by false precision. But the applied classroom task -- developing embodied non-verbal expression under live coaching -- remains outside AI's substitution range in the central case. Rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment rather than by any institutional lock, which stays only partial here.
THE 3231.d: This course for advanced performers explores character mask, neutral mask, half-mask and clowning. Mask characterization is the foundational tools in story-telling by communicating objectives, circumstances, and reactions through the body only.

r: Students here learn film terminology, camera-specific acting technique, auditioning for camera, and the practical demands of shooting -- an applied task set combining live, embodied performance with the technical literacy of working on set. Even so, the specific applied task in this course -- a human learning to control physical performance for a lens in real time -- is not itself replaced by that trend; a generative pipeline does not teach a student the skill, it competes with the finished product in the market. The wide uncertainty at this horizon concerns how much of the professional screen-acting field synthetic performers absorb, not whether embodied camera technique remains something only practiced human performance builds. Rating holds Low, protected by embodiment even as adjacent industry exposure clearly rises.
THE 3232.d: The student is introduced to the fundamental tools of acting for the camera. Students learn basic film terminology, specific camera-acting techniques, auditioning techniques, and the demands placed on an actor when shooting a film. The course uses exercises, scenes, and readings to provide a solid understanding of how to create a character, analyze a text, utilize important vocabulary, and perform effectively on camera.

Verification burden remains extreme: a coach's subjective, expert judgment of authenticity is the entire mechanism of the class, and that judgment is exactly the kind of non-obvious-failure evaluation the capability literature flags as resistant to automated review. The instrumental case for taking this culminating course stays Low across the horizon.

Even under a wide central case where synthetic performers are common in entertainment by 2036, the pedagogical function of an actor's lab -- building a human's capacity for truthful behavior under imaginary circumstances through supervised, repeated live practice -- is not a task AI performs for the student. Generative tools may increasingly produce finished performance artifacts, competing with actors in the labor market, but they cannot rehearse a student's instrument or supply the coached feedback loop this culminating course is built around. The genuine uncertainty at ten years is about the professional acting market's shape, not about whether this specific applied classroom task remains embodied and human-verified. Rating holds Low with high confidence in the mechanism, tempered honestly by not knowing how graduates will apply the skill professionally by 2036.
THE 3233.d: This course is the culminating class in the actor's journey. Students utilize all of their technique from previous shows and classes to focus on specific and intense scene work throughout the course. The focus of this class is learning to live and behave truthfully in imaginary circumstances.

THE 3234.d: This course is designed to cover the basics of audition techniques including film, realism, dance calls, cattle calls, cold reads, and various theatrical auditions. THE 3240.d: In this advanced performance course, students will explore basic improvisation acting techniques that enable the actor to develop concentration and spontaneity, build characterization, discover relationships and status, establish mood and feeling, sense shape and rhythm of scene and character, establish language and imagery, and build a play.

THE 3241.d: This is an introductory course for computer aided drafting for theatre. Students will become familiar with computer aided drafting software through theoretical and practical projects.
